Zoox Wins US Approval to Launch Paid Robotaxi in Las Vegas

FacebookXShare

Amazon’s Zoox will start charging for robotaxi rides in Las Vegas from August 10.

Listen to audio version of this article

0:00 / 4:08
Instaread

A robotaxi with no steering wheel and no pedals is about to carry paying passengers on US roads for the first time.

Amazon-owned Zoox announced this week that it will begin charging for rides in Las Vegas starting August 10, 2026. The launch marks the company’s first commercial operation, coming just days after federal regulators cleared the way for it to charge fares.

Zoox’s vehicle looks different from a typical car. It is an electric, carriage-style pod with two rows of seats facing each other. There is no steering wheel, no pedals, and no driver’s seat. The vehicle can reach speeds of up to 75 mph and was designed from the start for autonomous ride-hailing, rather than converted from an existing model.

Zoox has offered free rides in parts of Las Vegas, San Francisco, Austin, and Miami since last year as part of public testing. Starting August 10, riders in the Las Vegas Strip corridor will begin paying for those trips.

On July 30, 2026, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) granted Zoox a temporary exemption from federal rules that require vehicles to include human controls. This is the first exemption of its kind for a purpose-built autonomous vehicle without a steering wheel or pedals.

The exemption allows Zoox to operate up to 2,500 vehicles per year for two years. NHTSA said the approval includes an oversight structure that can adapt as the company’s technology develops.

Federal vehicle safety rules were written decades ago, when every car was assumed to have a human driver. This approval is one of the clearest signs yet that regulators are updating those rules for vehicles that do not need one.

Zoox has not disclosed its starting fare. The company said it plans to price rides close to the “Comfort” tier offered by other ride-hailing services, a level above standard economy options.

A few details on how pricing will work:

  • Fares will combine a base charge with time and distance, calculated using the best available route.
  • Fees tied to specific destinations, such as airport trips, will be shown to riders before booking.
  • Riders will not be charged extra if the vehicle ends up taking a longer route than planned.

Zoox CEO Aicha Evans has said that charging for rides brings a different kind of challenge than testing did, since paying customers expect more consistency than people taking a free ride.

The commercial launch puts Zoox up against established competitors. Alphabet’s Waymo already runs paid driverless rides in several US cities. Tesla has also started rolling out its own robotaxi service. Zoox now becomes a third major player racing to scale autonomous ride-hailing across the country.

Expanding beyond Nevada will take more work. Zoox still needs separate approval from state and local governments in each new market. Company leadership has said it is in talks with several state agencies, though not every state has welcomed the technology. New York, for example, dropped a proposal earlier this year that would have allowed commercial robotaxi service in parts of the state.

Robotaxi companies continue to face scrutiny over how their vehicles handle real-world situations, especially emergencies and interactions with other road users. Zoox has issued several software recalls over the past two years. The most recent came in July 2026, after one of its vehicles had trouble detecting heavy smoke near an emergency scene.

These incidents have not slowed Zoox’s rollout, but they are a reminder that the technology is still developing even as companies push toward wider commercial use.

Zoox was founded in 2014 to build a custom electric vehicle paired with its own self-driving system. Amazon acquired the company in 2020. The Las Vegas launch is the clearest sign yet that years of testing are turning into an actual business.

If the rollout goes well, Zoox is expected to seek approval for additional cities next. For now, the focus stays on Las Vegas, where paid rides begin on August 10.
